analysis.one_liner: Bans new oil, gas, and mineral leasing around Chaco Culture park and cancels idle leases.
analysis.headline: A bill to shield the land around Chaco Culture National Historical Park from new oil and gas drilling was introduced in the Senate's final weeks and died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have withdrawn federal land within the mapped area surrounding Chaco Culture National Historical Park from all new mining, oil and gas, and geothermal leasing, and would have automatically canceled federal oil and gas leases in that zone that were not producing. It left mineral rights on tribal trust and allotment land untouched and allowed the federal land to be conveyed to tribes. It was introduced late in the 117th Congress and never advanced past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Tribal nations with ancestral ties to the Chaco landscape — the Navajo Nation, Pueblo tribes, and the Hopi Tribe — along with residents of the Greater Chaco region, whom the bill's findings say have borne the health, safety, and quality-of-life effects of extensive natural gas development. Park visitors and the surrounding cultural landscape would also gain protection from renewed oil exploration in the Mancos/Gallup Shale play. The bill explicitly preserved mineral rights on tribal trust and allotment land and let the Secretary convey or exchange the withdrawn federal land with tribes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tribal nations and residents near Chaco Canyon

how_it_helps.text: Creates a permanent buffer by withdrawing federal land around the park from all new mineral, oil and gas, and geothermal leasing, blocking future drilling near an UNESCO World Heritage Site and its surrounding sacred sites.

Automatically terminates federal oil and gas leases in the buffer zone that have not been drilled and are not producing, so renewed interest in the Mancos/Gallup Shale play could not bring new development to the area around the park.

The bill's findings state that extensive natural gas development has affected the health, safety, economies, and quality of life of local communities, including the Navajo Nation, Pueblo tribes, and Hopi Tribe, and that a withdrawal would protect those communities and the park's resources.

Explicitly leaves tribal and Navajo allotment mineral rights untouched and permits the Secretary to convey or exchange the withdrawn land with tribes, so Native communities could gain land while existing tribal energy development continues.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding nonproducing federal leases inside the buffer zone lose those leases automatically. The withdrawal also forecloses future federal oil, gas, mining, and geothermal revenue and development in the area, which affects royalty income and energy-related economic activity in San Juan County, New Mexico.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas leaseholders near the park

drawbacks.text: Nonproducing oil and gas leases in the buffer zone terminate automatically and cannot be extended, wiping out leaseholders' existing positions and the possibility of future development on them.

The withdrawal is permanent, not time-limited, and covers all mineral leasing, mining, and geothermal development on the federal land, forfeiting federal mineral royalties and energy-related jobs in the region indefinitely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade-off is between protecting an irreplaceable archaeological and sacred landscape — and the health and quality of life of the tribal communities around it — and forgoing oil, gas, and mineral development on the federal land in the buffer. The economic cost falls on a concentrated group of leaseholders and on regional mineral revenue, while the bill deliberately spared tribal and allotment mineral owners, who keep full rights to develop their own land. On the merits it is a fairly conventional conservation withdrawal, but it arrived too late in the Congress to get a fair hearing.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the Senate's final weeks, the bill went to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico, joined by Senator Martin Heinrich, introduced the bill on November 17, 2022, less than seven weeks before the 117th Congress expired.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, which was its only action; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed.
The bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, leaving the buffer it would have created unenacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas leaseholders and operators in the area around Chaco Culture park are better off, because the legislative withdrawal and automatic lease terminations never took effect and the land remained open to leasing under existing law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas leaseholders near Chaco park

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were New Mexico Democrats and no Republican signed on, but the bill never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever tested.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers (San Juan Basin / Mancos-Gallup shale)
industries.note: Nonproducing federal leases in the buffer zone would terminate automatically, and the land would be permanently withdrawn from new leasing, blocking renewed oil exploration the bill's findings describe near the park. Their gain from continued access comes at the cost of the cultural landscape and nearby tribal communities.
The withdrawal removes the federal land from operation of the mining laws and the mineral materials and geothermal leasing laws, foreclosing those uses in the buffer.

industries.industry: Tribal and Navajo allotment mineral owners
industries.note: The bill expressly excludes trust and allotment land from the withdrawal, so tribal members' rights to develop their own minerals are fully preserved while the surrounding federal land is protected.
